title: Skip the Pull Request
one_liner: In agent-first delivery, gates in front of the integration merge replace the human pull-request review — the operator reads verdicts, not diffs.
problem: Pull-request review was designed for a scarcity that no longer holds: a human wrote the change slowly, and a second human reading it was the cheapest additional check available. Agent pipelines invert both halves. Change volume rises far past the rate at which anyone can read diffs, the author is a machine that can explain itself on demand, and the reviewer rarely carries the task context that made the change necessary. The queue becomes the bottleneck: batches grow, review degrades into rubber-stamped approval, and the pull request produces a compliance record rather than defect detection. Meanwhile the checks that actually discriminate — build, test suite, static analysis, security rules, spec conformance, architecture rules — are available before the merge and cost machine time instead of human attention. Keeping the pull request as the gate spends the scarcest resource on the weakest check, and frequently runs the strong checks after the merge, or not at all. There is a second, quieter problem: once nobody reads every diff, the word 'done' must mean something a machine can check, or the board fills with cards that claim delivery while the code sits on an unmerged branch.
solution: Move the accept-or-reject decision out of the pull request and in front of the integration merge, then give the human the verdict stream instead of the diff. Four things carry the weight. First, the platform owns git: the agent edits a worktree and never branches, commits or merges; the pipeline commits the run's changes and publishes them as an immutable, fenced delivery ref, so what gets reviewed is exactly what gets merged. Second, a deterministic gate: the delivery must build and pass the suite against the current integration head, and a red gate blocks integration without an argumentative override. Third, structured review over the delivery rather than over a bare diff: named review aspects return pass, concerns or block with findings and evidence pointers, while a separate code-review grade is kept as reporting evidence, never as a lane gate. A green delivery is integrated before a human sees it; the human-review lane then shows verdicts, evidence and the integration state, and a diff is opened on demand. Fourth, completion is a claim that requires proof: the integration state is recomputed from git ancestry of the commits attributed to the card, a card cannot reach the completed state while its delivery is not integrated, and an explicit operator override is the only exception and is recorded as such. Review and delivery writes carry fencing tokens, so a stale or superseded attempt cannot overwrite a newer one, and work rescued from a dying run lands on a salvage ref that is kept outside the review subject until someone consciously adopts it. Everything the pull request provided besides review is re-homed explicitly: the durable record moves into platform-owned task history and integration records, knowledge transfer and norms move into specs, decision records and living dossiers, and post-integration sweeps catch what per-change checks cannot see. Where an external rule demands a named human approver, keep a pull-request handoff as a configured integration strategy and run the same gates in front of it; the human then approves an already verified change.
